The title itself is the hook — it's not generic 'nutrition advice,' it's a targeted problem statement that speaks directly to coaches dealing with real client psychology. The phrase 'bad relationship with calorie counting' is loaded — it signals disordered eating history, anxiety around food tracking, and the coach's dilemma of needing data without causing harm. This framing attracts two audiences simultaneously: coaches who've had clients push back on tracking, and coaches who want to position themselves as more nuanced than the 'just count macros bro' crowd. The problem-solution title structure ('best options for X when Y') promises practical alternatives, not theory. It's also a topic most fitness content avoids because it requires nuance — most creators default to 'track everything' or 'intuitive eating only,' while this sits in the messy middle where real coaching happens. The specificity is what drove the outlier performance: generic nutrition videos get ignored, but a coach searching 'how to help a client who hates tracking' lands exactly here. The podcast format also signals depth — viewers expect a real conversation, not a 60-second hot take. This is a classic case of narrow topic + high emotional relevance + practical promise = outlier views in a small niche.
